closed_schools: North Star Elementary — closed end of 2024-25 (consolidated into East/Main).
Larsen Bay School — closed 2018 (<10 students); building transferred to the village in 2022.
Karluk School — closed 2 Nov 2023 (students moved to AKTEACH).
Danger Bay School — in 2015-16 SABS but not in NCES 2024-25; treated as closed.

gun position n of the battery
directing point — the precisely surveyed reference point used to compute the guns' firing data
Battery Commander's (Battery Command) station; in the annex's armament tables 'BC' after a gun also means barbette carriage
Plotting and Spotting Room
base end station 1 of Battery 3 / 6 (paired with spotting station S1/3 …)
base end station — an observation bunker or tower at one end of a baseline used to triangulate targets
Automatic Weapons Magazine
magazine (ammunition storage)
Battle Allowance magazine — the annex's name for the war-reserve ammunition stored in the harbor defenses
emplacement magazine
reserve magazine — probably the battery's Battle Allowance (war reserve) magazine
Fuze & Primer magazine
cantonment (label cut off) — the residential/camp section of a military installation
SCR-296-A — Army precision fire-control radar giving range and azimuth of ships to the plotting room
SCR-582 — fixed microwave harbor surveillance radar
searchlight (numbered as in Annex C: No. 1–26)
Distant Electric Control — the separate control station for a searchlight
Harbor Defense Observation Post (HDOP No. 3 was at Kizhuyak Point)
40 mm automatic weapon (gun)
probably anti-aircraft (the usual military abbreviation); no source checked describes these Buskin positions
orderly room — the administrative office of a small military unit
Fort Tidball (the Long Island fort of Batteries 4 and 5)
petroleum, oils and lubricants (fuel)
meaning not found in any source checked
meaning not found
prefixes on 'DUGOUT' / 'MAG' — meaning not found

properties.name: Fort J. H. Smith (WWII coast artillery)
properties.label: Fort J. H. Smith (WWII coast artillery)
properties.cat_label: Military history · location confidence medium
properties.rows:
What it wasWWII Army harbor-defense fort at Cape Chiniak / St. Peter's Head. Battery No. 1 mounted 8-inch guns at St. Peter's Head with a two-story underground ready-ammunition bunker. A gas-proof plotting/fire-control switchboard bunker (completed 24 Dec 1943) sits about 1,400 ft south of the 8-inch emplacement, with phone cables to the guns and Miller Field.Dates1942–WWII (plotting bunker completed 24 Dec 1943)UnitsCoast artillery; Battery G (searchlight), 250th Coast Artillery, per veteran accountWhat remainsGun emplacement/ammo bunker on the hill across the lagoon, plotting bunker, searchlight/control shelters (as of kadiak.org 1998–2000 visits).AccessOn Leisnoi Inc. land east of the end of state road maintenance — check 17(b) easements / Leisnoi permit rules. Bunkers can hold standing water.Coordinates57.62420, -152.19482Location confidencemedium — Point is the GNIS reference for the fort as a whole, not a specific gun.SourcesGNIS 'Fort J H Smith (historical)' via KIB geographic names layer; kadiak.org (Kodiak Military History Museum site, Joe Stevens) chiniak/command, chiniak/chinmap, units pages1944 Harbor Defense annexBattery No. 1 (construction No. 403), Fort J. H. Smith: two 8-inch guns on St. Peter's Head; emplacement completed 24 Dec 1943, with a lower floor added for storage and troop housing. Its BC station sat on top of the emplacement magazine; the plotting and spotting room (with the Fort J. H. Smith fire-control switchboard) was a separate dug-in concrete station. Battery No. 2 (155 mm, Chiniak Point) and the Round Top radar / Group No. 1 command post were also part of Fort J. H. Smith. Sources: 1944 Harbor Defense Project of Kodiak, Annex B (Fire Control), kadiak.org — http://www.kadiak.org/1944annex/annex_b.htmlField GPS (BAT1, 3 points)St. Peter's Head, Cape Chiniak. kadiak.org: 'St. Peters Head, Battery 1' (Fort J. H. Smith). The field-GPS points are about 37 m from this marker.
BAT1 EBC · 6 Aug 2011 · 141 ft
BAT1 GUN 2 · 6 Aug 2011 · 127 ft
BAT1 GUN1 · 6 Aug 2011 · 113 ft
Zoom in to see each point. Source: Field GPS survey (Datum WGS84)Old mapsThe Battery 1 gun circles (on the BAT1 field-GPS points), the U.S. Naval Reservation Boundary and the garrison building footprints from the kadiak.org Navy sheets chinmap2/chinmap3 are drawn on the map (Military layer). Source: kadiak.org (Kodiak Historical Army/Navy site)
properties.note: Old military sites can hold hazards (open bunkers, debris). Respect private/Native land.

UAF SuperDARN radar sits across the runway (not military).AccessReached from the end of the Chiniak Hwy; Leisnoi land — check easements.Coordinates57.61429, -152.19594Location confidencehighSourcesOSM way 641205098 (abandoned runway 'Miller Field'); kadiak.org (Kodiak Military History Museum site, Joe Stevens) chiniak tour (1998); Chiniak Area Comprehensive Plan 1987 (chiniak.org)Old mapsThe 'Steel Mat Runway – Miller Field' (about 1,420 m end to end on the old maps, longer than today's strip) and the Flight Clearance Lines are drawn on the map from kadiak.org chinmap2/chinmap3. properties.name: Cape Greville fire-control station / CG radio beacon

properties.cat_label: Military history · location confidence medium
properties.rows: What it was40-acre harbor-defense site (acquired 29 Aug 1941) for the B3/2 fire-control station spotting for the 155 mm battery at Chiniak Point. properties.label: Round Top — structures (unlabelled)
properties.cat_label: Military history · from an old map · structure
properties.rows:
SummaryProbably the WWII Round Top radar site (SCR-296A) and Group No. 1 postWhat it was• Round Top had an SCR-296A radar tower (its radome disguised as a wooden water tank), a metal radar equipment building, a Quonset and a wooden water tower — documented [1]
• The Group No. 1 command and observation post on Round Top was a 50-foot wooden tower completed 17 Nov 1943; the SCR-296 there served Battery No. 1 — documented [2]
• These are the three structures at the end of the Round Top loop road, where the radar site is — likely, from building shape and positionTermsSCR296 = SCR-296-A — Army precision fire-control radar giving range and azimuth of ships to the plotting room (confirmed [3][2])Sources[1] kadiak.org, Round Top radar site — https://www.kadiak.org/chiniak/scr296.html

SummaryProbably D-2 (barracks / operations) and D-3 (garage / power plant) of the Navy stationWhat it was• 1965 list: D-2 communications building (communications 792 sf, enlisted men's barracks with mess 8,052 sf, administration 700 sf, cold storage 1,000 sf); D-3 auto maintenance garage (garage 1,572 sf, transmitter 457 sf, water supply & treatment, heating plant 800 sf, diesel-electric power plant 1,008 sf, 75 kV standby generator) — documented [1]
• The main building was a two-story barracks / operations building near the beach (barracks, rec room / mess, operations with communications gear, OIC rooms); the engineering / generator / garage building stood 20–30 yards away and parallel, with three generator exhaust ports — documented [2]
• The two long buildings at the centre of the station match these two — likely, from building shape and positionSources[1] 1965 Navy structure list, U.S. Naval Station Kodiak (kadiak.org) — https://www.kadiak.org/navy/structures.html

properties.name: Steel Mat Runway – Miller Field
properties.label: Steel Mat Runway – Miller Field
properties.cat_label: Military history · from an old map · runway
properties.rows:
SummaryMiller Field — WWII runway of Marston (pierced steel plank) mattingAlso onU.S. Navy Chiniak sheet — garrison & landing strip (kadiak.org chinmap3)What it was• Marston mat (pierced steel planking) was developed just before WWII for rapid temporary runways — documented [1]
• At Miller Field the mats run lengthwise along the runway — said to be the wrong way; about half remains, much of it buried; each section about 66 lb, 10 ft × 15 in — documented [2]
• In 1998 the runway was badly potholed and not usable for aircraft; the USCG put a DGPS transmitter beside it c. 1997 — documented [2]Sources[1] Wikipedia, Marston Mat — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marston_Mat
[2] kadiak.org, Chiniak tour — https://www.kadiak.org/chiniak/chiniak.htmlOn the mapLabelled 'STEEL MAT RUNWAY - MILLER FIELD' (chinmap2) and 'PIERCED STEEL MAT LANDING STRIP …' (chinmap3; the length/lease text is too small to read). Drawn end to end as on the 1949 USGS map (about 1,420 m, longer than today's strip).Source mapU.S. Navy Chiniak sheet — Miller Field / Battery 1 (kadiak.org chinmap2)Approx. accuracy± 50 m — traced by hand from a scanned mapHow it was placedfitted to the Battery 1 gun GPS points, the 1949 USGS runway ends and the shoreline (GCP residuals 11, 5, 49, 0 m)Sourcekadiak.org (Kodiak Historical Army/Navy site)
properties.note: Old military sites can hold hazards (open bunkers, debris). Respect private/Native land.

properties.cat_label: Military history · from an old map · boundary
properties.rows:
SummaryBoundary of the Chiniak Air Force tracking station landWhat it was• The Air Force began the AC&W site in 1956; converted to a space tracking station two years later — documented [1]
• Closure announced to the station's 123 employees in March 1975 — documented [2]Sources[1] Chiniak Area Comprehensive Plan 1987 (kadiak.org) — https://www.kadiak.org/chiniak/chiniakplan1987.html
[2] kadiak.org, Air Force Tracking Station at Chiniak — https://www.kadiak.org/af_track/af.htmlOn the mapBoundary labelled 'U.S. AIR FORCE INSTALLATION 226.7 Acres NOY(R)-54765' and 'U.S. AIR FORCE BOUNDARY'. The north and east corners are drawn on the map; the west and south corners run off the sheet and are completed from the edge directions and the 226.7 acres. The 1949 USGS map shows a dashed 'Coast Guard Reservation' square in the same place.Source mapU.S. Air Force installation map, Chiniak (kadiak.org chinmap5)Approx. accuracy± 35 m — traced by hand from a scanned mapHow it was placedfitted to the pond and lake outlines (OpenStreetMap); boundary agrees with the 1949 USGS 'Coast Guard Reservation' within ~50 mSourcekadiak.org (Kodiak Historical Army/Navy site)

SummaryBattery 3 base end station B1/3 (Gibson Cove)What it was• B1/3, S1/3 on Site 9, Gibson Cove, Fort Greely: a reinforced-concrete, dug-in, splinter-proof OP completed 17 Nov 1943 — documented [1]
• Battery No. 3 (F 42-6), Fort Greely: four 155 mm guns on Panama mounts on Buskin Hill, completed Oct 1942; by 1944 the guns were in central storage at Fort Greely — documented [2][1]TermsBES = base end station — an observation bunker or tower at one end of a baseline used to triangulate targets (confirmed [3][1])
B1/3, B1/6 … = base end station 1 of Battery 3 / 6 (paired with spotting station S1/3 …) (confirmed [1][3])Sources[1] 1944 Harbor Defense Project of Kodiak, Annex B (Fire Control), kadiak.org — http://www.kadiak.org/1944annex/annex_b.html
[2] 1944 Harbor Defense Project of Kodiak, Annex A (Armament), kadiak.org — http://www.kadiak.org/1944annex/annex_a.html
[3] Wikipedia, Base end station — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_end_stationLabelGibson Cove BES (as recorded)Survey datenot recordedAltitudenot recordedCoordinatesN57 46 31.7 W152 27 14.6  =  57.775472, -152.454056SourceField GPS survey (Datum WGS84) — the same list appears on kadiak.org maps.html marked NAD83 (≈1 m from WGS84 here)
